en.content:
The Tai Po fire that claimed lives has left more than physical damage—it has disrupted families’ ability to retrieve belongings and begin the difficult work of rebuilding. One resident’s call for “better arrangements” to collect personal items, and for a longer window to visit flats, speaks to a basic, humane expectation: that the government’s response should be practical and compassionate, not only procedural. In emergencies, details matter. A narrow timetable can turn grief into an added burden, especially for elderly victims, people with limited mobility, or those who must balance work and caregiving while dealing with investigations.

At the same time, it is important to recognise why authorities may set limits: safety assessments, forensic checks, and the need to control access in unstable buildings. These steps are not obstacles to be brushed aside; they are part of responsible governance. Yet responsibility also means calibrating measures to real social needs. Where hazards are being managed and units are still under assessment, authorities can still provide structured pathways—extended visiting hours, staggered collection schedules, clear signage and staff support, and assistance for those unable to attend in person.

The public discussion around the Tai Po blaze should therefore focus less on blame in the abstract and more on system design after tragedy. A clearer framework for post-incident recovery—covering timelines for residents to retrieve personal effects, communication channels in multiple languages and for vulnerable groups, and coordination between departments—would reduce confusion and the risk that survivors feel neglected. Transparent explanations of what is within and outside the government’s control, paired with concrete improvements, can help rebuild trust.

Ultimately, the most significant test is whether the city treats victims as citizens first. Beyond the immediate scene, the government’s credibility will be measured by whether it can convert lessons from the disaster into better assistance for residents in the weeks ahead. If the administration can respond to requests for more time and better arrangements with sincerity and efficiency, it will not only ease suffering but also demonstrate that the goal of public safety extends to protecting dignity, not just preventing further harm.

zh.content:
啟德醫院地盤工傷死亡事件，再次把「職安健」放到最刺眼的位置。59歲工人喺重型工程部件下遇事，唔單止係個人悲劇，更係整個承建、監管同外判鏈條嘅問責考題。社會最需要唔係「例行公關式」交代，而係一套徹底、可驗證、可追責嘅調查：死因機制點解會發生、風險評估做過冇、現場安全標準係唔係符合合約同法規、以及責任邊個承擔——尤其當事故涉及多層承判時，責任更容易被「逐層稀釋」。

值得留意嘅另一層面係現場安全文化。近期太埔火災調查亦提到部分消防風險項目可能唔屬消防處「範圍」；但即使話有部門界線，工人生命安全唔可以被框架切割。職安健制度本質係「全面風險管理」——包括工程管理、作業程序、設備狀態、工序銜接、以及臨場監督。若當局只用「唔係我範疇」去分散焦點，結果就會係事故一再發生、同樣問題一再被證實存在，卻仍無法真正改變現場做法。

因此，勞工團體要求政府作「徹底」調查，方向正確，因為徹底意味住：唔止要交代「發生咩」，仲要交代「為何容許發生」；唔止要檢討單次疏忽，更要檢視制度是否存在系統性漏洞，例如承建商安全評核機制是否真能落地、對違規行為嘅阻嚇力夠唔夠、以及事故後有冇跟進改善成效嘅監察。社會亦有權期待調查結果能轉化成硬措施：包括針對相同工種、相同工序嘅即時風險管控要求，以及對屢犯者採取更具體嘅制裁路徑。

同時，對工人同家屬而言，「調查」唔係抽象承諾；要同步處理賠償、支援、以及對後續工作安排嘅安排，否則只會令生命代價變成另一場行政程序。香港一向自詡法治同專業監管，面對具體死亡個案，最重要係用證據說話、用機制補洞、用問責落實。願政府今次唔止做到「查清楚」，更做到「改得了」，否則每一次悲劇都只會成為制度迴避責任嘅代價。

A survivor of the deadly Tai Po fire has urged the government to make better arrangements for residents to retrieve personal belongings and allow a longer time to visit their flats.



Jason Kong, a resident at the fire-ravaged Wang Fuk Court and former member of the estate owners’ corporation, told local media on Thursday that his family did not have enough time to search for, collect and pack all their personal belongings within the designated three hours.
